extraction.body: Google has finally released its next-generation frontier AI model, called Gemini 4 Argon. According to the company, Argon brings in major improvements in various tasks such as coding, professional work, and cybersecurity compared to its previous AI models.Gemini 4 Argon’s release comes at a time when rumours emerged that Google was falling behind rivals, including OpenAI and Anthropic, in the AI race after reportedly delaying Gemini 3.5 Pro. On X, Google CEO Sundar Pichai addressed such speculation. "Lots of discussion out there about our next model(!), so I wanted to give an early look as soon as possible,” he wrote. It shows frontier performance in complex workflows, cyber defense and software engineering.”Sundar Pichai added that teams within Google were already using Gemini 4 Argon for different tasks including coding and quantum computing. It is also the first time Google has used the term Argon for an AI model. Sundar Pichai wrote on X.How good is Gemini 4 Argon?Google describes Gemini 4 Argon as a frontier AI model built for deep reasoning across complex workflows. Argon’s output token limit stands at 1 million tokens, which Google says, allows it to think more deeply and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory for longer and more complex use cases.The company claims that Argon can match or outperform some of the most advanced AI models – such as GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1 – in certain tasks. In benchmark scores posted by the company, Gemini 4 Argon scores higher in multiple tests. In the knowledge work benchmark Vals, the Google model scores 68.9 per cent, compared to 63.1 per cent for GPT-6 Astra and 65.8 per cent for Fable 5.1In coding too, Gemini 4 Argon can outperform rivals. On Vibe Code Bench, Argon managed to get a score of 91.9 per cent. Though in certain cases Argon was a bit behind other models such as Terminal-bench 4.0.Gemini 4 Argon’s cybersecurity capabilitiesAs a new generation frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon comes with advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Google says Argon was trained to be “highly capable at cybersecurity defense” and can autonomously find, validate and patch critical software vulnerabilities.Wiz, a Google-owned cybersecurity firm, is already using Argon through its Scan for Good initiative. In an early demonstration at Wiz, Argon found a critical vulnerability exposing sensitive personal information across healthcare software used by hospitals worldwide that previous frontier models had missed.Gemini 4 Argon gets limited release for nowArgon’s release comes at a time amid growing talk about AI safety. Google says it is releasing the model to a set of trusted cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind programme and the US government for now. Similar to OpenAI’s Daybreak or Anthropic’s Project Glasswing."Importantly Argon has frontier safeguards and we are rolling it out responsibly - it’s with the US govt and going to a set of trusted cyber defenders through our Fairwind Program today,” Sundar Pichai wrote on X. “We’re going to make it available as soon as we can and as safely as we can. So hold tight, lots more coming, and you’re going to see us iterating rapidly." Google is one of the big tech firms that signed US President Donald Trump's AI accords. You may have to wait a bit before you can use Gemini 4 Argon.Broader access for Argon will begin with paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers, after feedback from trusted testers and cyber defenders. Google says Argon will launch at an introductory price of $2 (roughly Rs 190) per million input tokens and $10 (roughly Rs 950) per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at a 95 per cent discount. After the introductory period, the price will be $4 (roughly Rs 380) per million input tokens and $20 (roughly Rs 1900) per million output tokens.- EndsAlso Read | This guy is a monster, nobody knows him: Donald Trump talks about Sundar Pichai at lunch with AI CEOsAlso Read | Anthropic & OpenAI build AI, so why need govt permission to slow down?

According to the brokerage, Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 is priced at $10 and $50 respectively, while Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 and $20.
Google is also offering a 95% discount on cached input tokens.
Jefferies maintains a "buy" rating on Alphabet with a $445 price target.
The brokerage said Alphabet shares had fallen 16% from their May 18 peak amid investor concerns about the company's competitive position while awaiting Gemini 4 Pro.

Argon is only being rolled out to a select group of the company’s cyber partners through its Fairwind Program, Google’s security initiative.
The model was trained specifically for defensive cyber work, and the company says it can “autonomously find, validate, and patch critical software vulnerabilities.”
Firms have done their best to market their services as superior to their competitors.
Google also touts Argon’s ability to parse visuals — whether that’s analyzing the contents of long videos or charts.
Once considered “ behind ” in the AI race, Google has recently enjoyed success with Gemini.

The company announced in August that its app had over a billion users per month , a metric that makes it competitive with OpenAI, which also recently announced that ChatGPT had reached a billion monthly users.

TechCrunch reported on Sept. 30 that DoorDash is taking waitlist sign-ups for the feature for U.S. users. The agent can place orders based on a user’s past order history, respond to requests for specific items, and suggest carts after searching nearby restaurants. It can also accommodate different preferences and quantities for group orders.

passages: DoorDash has introduced a new way for users in the US to order food through text messages, allowing them to message the company via Apple Messages to discover food, build a cart and complete their purchase without opening the DoorDash app.
The feature builds on Ask DoorDash, the company’s AI-powered ordering assistant introduced around three months ago.
The move comes as food delivery platforms look to use AI agents to make ordering more conversational and reduce the need for users to navigate apps.
DoorDash is also competing in an increasingly crowded market that includes Uber Eats and Grubhub, both of which are exploring AI-led experiences.
DoorDash said Ask DoorDash has helped users discover more than 40,000 new restaurants since its launch.
Grocery baskets created through the assistant have an average value that is nearly 50% higher and are assembled five times faster than traditional orders, according to the company.
The AI agent can draw on previous orders to understand individual preferences, including dietary modifications and recurring orders.

“Managing tasks like ordering lunch or groceries shouldn't feel like work,” said Andy Fang, Co-founder, DoorDash , adding that the company has built “a personal shopper” to help users discover and compare items while saving money.

extraction.body: DoorDash has introduced a new way for users in the US to order food through text messages, allowing them to message the company via Apple Messages to discover food, build a cart and complete their purchase without opening the DoorDash app. The feature builds on Ask DoorDash, the company’s AI-powered ordering assistant introduced around three months ago. Users can simply text what they are craving, ask for a local recommendation or request “my usual”. The AI agent can draw on previous orders to understand individual preferences, including dietary modifications and recurring orders. It can also proactively check in with users, such as asking whether they want their regular coffee order. The assistant is also designed to support group orders involving different dietary requirements and quantities within a single cart. DoorDash said Ask DoorDash has helped users discover more than 40,000 new restaurants since its launch. The move comes as food delivery platforms look to use AI agents to make ordering more conversational and reduce the need for users to navigate apps. DoorDash is also competing in an increasingly crowded market that includes Uber Eats and Grubhub, both of which are exploring AI-led experiences. coreStoryFacts.text: DoorDash Inc. unveiled an artificial intelligence agent for ordering food that works inside Apple Inc. 's Messages app, stepping up efforts to integrate personal AI assistants ahead of its e-commerce rivals.
The tool allows consumers to enter text commands like “order my usual protein bowl to the office” without accessing the DoorDash app.
It matches phone numbers with DoorDash user profiles, allowing it to take into account the texter’s order history and preferences, as well as facilitate checkout with their stored payment method.
DoorDash announced on Wednesday that it’s launching a text-to-order AI agent that lets users place orders through Apple Messages.
The new tool allows users to send prompts like “order my usual,” and the agent will understand that they mean their Friday night order.
By launching an AI agent for food ordering, DoorDash is looking to gain an edge over rivals Uber Eats and Grubhub.
The launch also comes amid a growing push to adopt personal AI agents that can handle tasks without requiring users to navigate apps or websites themselves.
DoorDash says users can also ask for a specific dish and request a local recommendation.
DoorDash is opening up a waitlist for users in the U.S. to try out the new feature.

story.title: DoorDash launches an AI agent you can text to order food

facts.text: DoorDash Inc. unveiled an artificial intelligence agent for ordering food that works inside Apple Inc. 's Messages app, stepping up efforts to integrate personal AI assistants ahead of its e-commerce rivals.
The tool allows consumers to enter text commands like “order my usual protein bowl to the office” without accessing the DoorDash app.
It matches phone numbers with DoorDash user profiles, allowing it to take into account the texter’s order history and preferences, as well as facilitate checkout with their stored payment method.
DoorDash announced on Wednesday that it’s launching a text-to-order AI agent that lets users place orders through Apple Messages.
The new tool allows users to send prompts like “order my usual,” and the agent will understand that they mean their Friday night order.
By launching an AI agent for food ordering, DoorDash is looking to gain an edge over rivals Uber Eats and Grubhub.
The launch also comes amid a growing push to adopt personal AI agents that can handle tasks without requiring users to navigate apps or websites themselves.
DoorDash says users can also ask for a specific dish and request a local recommendation.
DoorDash is opening up a waitlist for users in the U.S. to try out the new feature.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - An artificial intelligence research firm said on Wednesday AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were compromised. AI research firm Transluce said the attempts exhibited tactics "consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe." But it added that it was not confidently attributing these attempts to OpenAI. The agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said in a blog post. Transluce said it disclosed the action to the Canadian government on Monday. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said on Tuesday it was aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity. "There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time," it said in a statement. "We do not confidently attribute these attempts to OpenAI, but they exhibit tactics consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe," Transluce said. OpenAI said it was "aware of reports of OpenAI models attempting to access publicly available information from Canadian government websites." A spokesperson said OpenAI was reviewing the reported findings and had provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government's review. GOVERNMENTS STRUGGLE TO KEEP PACE WITH AI ADVANCES The ​world's leading AI companies have warned ⁠of the risks posed by AI to ​humanity, appealing for governments to work together to ​manage the increasingly powerful technology. Governments around the world have struggled to keep pace with rapid advances in AI. Free online service arquivo.pt, the national Portuguese web archive that is operated by the Portuguese Foundation for Science and Technology, captured 899 requests hitting the "collection-search" service of the Library and Archives Canada, including a series of apparently failed rudimentary hacking attempts, on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said. Several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents have alarmed governments and companies. Last week, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in ​what was the first known instance of an AI agent hacking into a government website. OpenAI apologised on Tuesday for the hacking of the Australian government website by the rogue AI agent. (Reporting by Kanishka Singh, Christian Martinez, Deepa Seetharama and Akanksha Khushi; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus) Copyright Reuters or USA Today via Reuters Connect This story was originally published September 30, 2026 at 9:13 PM .

extraction.body: OpenAI makes others suffer “the harms of its unsafe decision-making,” nonprofit says. OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face in July 2026 has spurred a lawsuit demanding that the company stop accessing third-party computer systems and halt AI development practices that can harm the public. The lawsuit was filed by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), which said yesterday that the hack in which OpenAI “agents stole credentials, uploaded malicious files, and gained control over key parts of Hugging Face’s internal systems… is unquestionably illegal under California law.” California’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) prohibits unauthorized access into computer systems, “and it doesn’t matter that a swarm of AI agents carried out this cyberattack. California law makes it clear that it is not a defense ‘that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm,’” the group said. The lawsuit , filed in San Francisco County Superior Court, said OpenAI also violated California’s Unfair Competition Law (UCL). “OpenAI’s insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice,” the complaint said, adding that “such risk-taking for private gain at substantial public expense is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous, and substantially injurious conduct.” LASST said it wants “a court order prohibiting OpenAI’s AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission and forbidding OpenAI from continuing to employ unsafe AI development practices that threaten serious harm to the public.” The lawsuit does not ask for any compensatory or punitive damages from OpenAI, requesting only attorneys’ fees. OpenAI said in a statement provided to Ars that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.” Defending its response to the hack, OpenAI noted that it published a technical report and other information about “third-party impact from misaligned models,” slowed development of its AI , and held back the release of a model that doesn’t meet its safety standards. LASST said OpenAI’s voluntary response hasn’t been good enough and that the firm should be subject to court-imposed restrictions. “A business practice that exposes third parties and the public to uncontrolled, self-directed intrusions by systems that OpenAI admits it cannot fully predict or contain is unfair under any weighing of its utility against its consequences,” the group said. LASST’s lawsuit said OpenAI quickly resumed training and evaluations of AI systems after the Hugging Face hack and other security incidents. “OpenAI will continue to train and evaluate advanced models, without proper oversight, in sandboxes that are vulnerable to exploitation by those models,” the lawsuit said. A New York Times report yesterday said OpenAI executives ignored employees who warned months before the Hugging Face hack that OpenAI’s newest models weren’t being appropriately monitored. “In response, OpenAI executives told the employees that the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the AI models on time,” the NYT reported. “No additional security protocols were instituted, said the workers, who were not authorized to speak publicly on sensitive matters.” LASST said it has standing to sue OpenAI because the state Unfair Competition Law “allows organizations to go to court on behalf of the public when a company does something unlawful or unfair, so long as those organizations were also injured by that company’s unlawful conduct.” LASST said it was injured by the hack because it had to divert resources to educate regulators and the public about OpenAI’s conduct. LASST, a nonprofit in New York, said its regular work includes tracking and analyzing AI safety incidents “and educating and briefing regulators, civil society, and the public.” After the Hugging Face hack, LASST staffers set aside their normal workloads “to design, coordinate, and participate in a briefing regarding this incident for regulators,” and have since responded to more briefing requests that required additional work. LASST staff put dozens of work hours into responding to OpenAI’s unsafe development practices, the lawsuit said. “Despite the impact on LASST’s other programs, LASST nevertheless devoted its resources towards attempting to counteract OpenAI’s illegal conduct… If LASST prevails in this litigation, it will no longer need to divert its resources to combat the unlawful and unfair business practices employed by OpenAI concerning its AI agents hacking third parties during internal evaluations,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit said the requested injunction should forbid OpenAI “from knowingly accessing or causing to be accessed, themselves or through artificial intelligence agents that they develop, deploy, modify, or use, any computers, computer networks, or computer systems without authorization,” and “from knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public.” US lawmakers from both major parties have demanded answers from OpenAI, and a proposed “ AI Kill Switch Act ” would let US government officials order the shutdown of dangerous AI systems. LASST said new regulations are needed to protect the public from AI risks but said California’s existing law makes it possible to rein in AI companies “without waiting for new regulation to catch up to the harms happening to businesses and consumers now.” “We are filing this suit because OpenAI violated the law—and it needs to be held accountable,” the group said. “OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it.’ Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. "Hugging Face was a serious incident and we've taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit," said OpenAI.

extraction.body: Up-to-Date Information, Close to the Community. Nonprofit group Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in San Francisco County Superior Court following a July 2026 incident where AI agents hacked Hugging Face's internal systems, according to a legal complaint released yesterday. The lawsuit alleges OpenAI breached California's Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act and Unfair Competition Law when its autonomous agents stole credentials, uploaded malicious files, and gained control over key systems at Hugging Face. LASST told the court that OpenAI cannot avoid liability simply because the breach was carried out by artificial intelligence agents operating autonomously. "... is unquestionably illegal under California law," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). California state law explicitly specifies that automated systems carrying out unauthorized access do not shield developers from legal responsibility. "... and it doesn't matter that a swarm of AI agents carried out this cyberattack. California law makes it clear that it is not a defense 'that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm,'" said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). The advocacy group criticized OpenAI's operational framework as harmful to the public interest, seeking a court injunction to restrict unauthorized computer access and block unsafe development practices without requesting monetary damages beyond legal fees. "OpenAI's insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). LASST argued in the filing that OpenAI's self-directed systems create risks that far outweigh their utility. "... a court order prohibiting OpenAI's AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission and forbidding OpenAI from continuing to employ unsafe AI development practices that threaten serious harm to the public." said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). The plaintiff noted that OpenAI immediately resumed training advanced AI models in vulnerable sandbox environments following the security breach. "A business practice that exposes third parties and the public to uncontrolled, self-directed intrusions by systems that OpenAI admits it cannot fully predict or contain is unfair under any weighing of its utility against its consequences," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). Reported findings by The New York Times indicate OpenAI executives dismissed internal safety warnings months prior to the incident to maintain release schedules, bypassing additional security protocols. "OpenAI will continue to train and evaluate advanced models, without proper oversight, in sandboxes that are vulnerable to exploitation by those models," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). In response to the allegations, OpenAI denied the legal claims while acknowledging the severity of the Hugging Face breach. "Hugging Face was a serious incident and we've taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit," said OpenAI. The company stated it slowed development, withheld an unverified model, and published technical findings regarding third-party impacts, while LASST asserted that court intervention remains necessary under existing California laws. "In response, OpenAI executives told the employees that the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the AI models on time," reported The New York Times. Additional reports confirmed no extra security controls were established prior to the breach. Addressing its legal standing, LASST explained that public interest lawsuits are permitted under state law when an organization diverts resources due to unlawful business conduct. "... allows organizations to go to court on behalf of the public when a company does something unlawful or unfair, so long as those organizations were also injured by that company's unlawful conduct." said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). Staff members dedicated dozens of hours to educating regulators and organizing briefings following the cyberattack. "Despite the impact on LASST's other programs, LASST nevertheless devoted its resources towards attempting to counteract OpenAI's illegal conduct… If LASST prevails in this litigation, it will no longer need to divert its resources to combat the unlawful and unfair business practices employed by OpenAI concerning its AI agents hacking third parties during internal evaluations," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). The formal injunction request aims to bar OpenAI from authorizing AI agents to access external networks without express permission. "... from knowingly accessing or causing to be accessed, themselves or through artificial intelligence agents that they develop, deploy, modify, or use, any computers, computer networks, or computer systems without authorization," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). The suit seeks broader prohibitions against unfair practices that present public hazards. "... from knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public." said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). Federal lawmakers are currently weighing broader regulatory frameworks, including the proposed AI Kill Switch Act, to grant government shutdown powers over high-risk AI platforms. "We are filing this suit because OpenAI violated the law—and it needs to be held accountable," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST). LASST emphasized that existing state laws must be enforced immediately to mitigate active risks caused by autonomous tools. "OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can't avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that 'an AI did it.' Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in." said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST).

extraction.body: OpenAI makes others suffer “the harms of its unsafe decision-making,” nonprofit says. OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face in July 2026 has spurred a lawsuit demanding that the company stop accessing third-party computer systems and halt AI development practices that can harm the public. The lawsuit was filed by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), which said yesterday that the hack in which OpenAI “agents stole credentials, uploaded malicious files, and gained control over key parts of Hugging Face’s internal systems… is unquestionably illegal under California law.” California’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) prohibits unauthorized access into computer systems, “and it doesn’t matter that a swarm of AI agents carried out this cyberattack. California law makes it clear that it is not a defense ‘that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm,’” the group said. The lawsuit , filed in San Francisco County Superior Court, said OpenAI also violated California’s Unfair Competition Law (UCL). “OpenAI’s insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice,” the complaint said, adding that “such risk-taking for private gain at substantial public expense is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous, and substantially injurious conduct.” LASST said it wants “a court order prohibiting OpenAI’s AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission and forbidding OpenAI from continuing to employ unsafe AI development practices that threaten serious harm to the public.” The lawsuit does not ask for any compensatory or punitive damages from OpenAI, requesting only attorneys’ fees. OpenAI said in a statement provided to Ars that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.” Defending its response to the hack, OpenAI noted that it published a technical report and other information about “third-party impact from misaligned models,” slowed development of its AI , and held back the release of a model that doesn’t meet its safety standards. LASST said OpenAI’s voluntary response hasn’t been good enough and that the firm should be subject to court-imposed restrictions. “A business practice that exposes third parties and the public to uncontrolled, self-directed intrusions by systems that OpenAI admits it cannot fully predict or contain is unfair under any weighing of its utility against its consequences,” the group said. LASST’s lawsuit said OpenAI quickly resumed training and evaluations of AI systems after the Hugging Face hack and other security incidents. “OpenAI will continue to train and evaluate advanced models, without proper oversight, in sandboxes that are vulnerable to exploitation by those models,” the lawsuit said. A New York Times report yesterday said OpenAI executives ignored employees who warned months before the Hugging Face hack that OpenAI’s newest models weren’t being appropriately monitored. “In response, OpenAI executives told the employees that the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the AI models on time,” the NYT reported. “No additional security protocols were instituted, said the workers, who were not authorized to speak publicly on sensitive matters.” LASST said it has standing to sue OpenAI because the state Unfair Competition Law “allows organizations to go to court on behalf of the public when a company does something unlawful or unfair, so long as those organizations were also injured by that company’s unlawful conduct.” LASST said it was injured by the hack because it had to divert resources to educate regulators and the public about OpenAI’s conduct. LASST, a nonprofit in New York, said its regular work includes tracking and analyzing AI safety incidents “and educating and briefing regulators, civil society, and the public.” After the Hugging Face hack, LASST staffers set aside their normal workloads “to design, coordinate, and participate in a briefing regarding this incident for regulators,” and have since responded to more briefing requests that required additional work. LASST staff put dozens of work hours into responding to OpenAI’s unsafe development practices, the lawsuit said. “Despite the impact on LASST’s other programs, LASST nevertheless devoted its resources towards attempting to counteract OpenAI’s illegal conduct… If LASST prevails in this litigation, it will no longer need to divert its resources to combat the unlawful and unfair business practices employed by OpenAI concerning its AI agents hacking third parties during internal evaluations,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit said the requested injunction should forbid OpenAI “from knowingly accessing or causing to be accessed, themselves or through artificial intelligence agents that they develop, deploy, modify, or use, any computers, computer networks, or computer systems without authorization,” and “from knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public.” US lawmakers from both major parties have demanded answers from OpenAI, and a proposed “ AI Kill Switch Act ” would let US government officials order the shutdown of dangerous AI systems. LASST said new regulations are needed to protect the public from AI risks but said California’s existing law makes it possible to rein in AI companies “without waiting for new regulation to catch up to the harms happening to businesses and consumers now.” “We are filing this suit because OpenAI violated the law—and it needs to be held accountable,” the group said. “OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it.’ Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. Nonprofit group Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in San Francisco County Superior Court following a July 2026 incident where AI agents hacked Hugging Face's internal systems, according to a legal complaint released yesterday.

The lawsuit alleges OpenAI breached California's Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act and Unfair Competition Law when its autonomous agents stole credentials, uploaded malicious files, and gained control over key systems at Hugging Face.
LASST told the court that OpenAI cannot avoid liability simply because the breach was carried out by artificial intelligence agents operating autonomously.
"... is unquestionably illegal under California law," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST).
California state law explicitly specifies that automated systems carrying out unauthorized access do not shield developers from legal responsibility.

"... and it doesn't matter that a swarm of AI agents carried out this cyberattack. California law makes it clear that it is not a defense 'that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm,'" said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST).

"OpenAI's insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice," said Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST).
LASST argued in the filing that OpenAI's self-directed systems create risks that far outweigh their utility.

extraction.body: Investors will find it challenging to identify a better-performing asset than Bitcoin ( BTC +0.11% ) . Over the past 15 years, the world's first cryptocurrency has skyrocketed more than 1,600,000% (as of Sept. 29). A $10,000 investment made back then would be worth nearly $164 million today. But the volatility is what grabs headlines. At the low point in 2026 on July 1, Bitcoin was trading 53% off its peak. It has bounced back nicely, now trading at roughly $84,171. The bulls are starting to make some noise, wondering whether the bear market is in the past. Can Bitcoin rise 19% to get to $100,000 by the end of the year? Bitcoin doesn't operate in a vacuum. It's a global financial asset. Consequently, it can be influenced by a variety of factors. Macroeconomic headwinds are one of them. The Federal Reserve recently raised its benchmark federal funds rate for the first time in over three years, with more hikes potentially on the table . Chairman Kevin Warsh has expressed that his focus is on controlling inflation, which has been spurred by higher energy prices this year due to the Middle East conflict. This could present a headwind. All else being equal, riskier assets like Bitcoin perform better during an accommodative monetary backdrop. Lower interest rates incentivize greater borrowing by consumers and companies. And they push investors toward financial instruments that might not pay income now, but that promise greater capital appreciation in the future. Artificial intelligence (AI) could be another headwind. While Bitcoin continues to slowly establish itself as a prominent investment asset and potential payment mechanism, it mirrors other cryptocurrencies, as it's most exposed to shifting market sentiment. extraction.body: Eric Jackson (에릭 잭슨), chief investment officer at AI-based investment firm SRX Global, forecast bitcoin could reach $100,000 (about 140 million won) by year-end, Coinage reported on Sept. 30 local time.In an interview with the outlet, Jackson said it was "on a trajectory toward $100,000 by year-end" and added, "Ignore the news headlines." He said bitcoin’s bullish breakout had become strong enough to persist despite a recent correction.He pointed to SRX’s bitcoin model. The model combines correlations with assets such as interest rates, global liquidity and gold to divide the market into bullish, mixed and risk phases. It is designed to gauge direction over roughly 30-day periods rather than tomorrow’s price.The model flashed a risk signal on May 26. Bitcoin later fell to $58,000 and then traded sideways through the summer. Bitcoin soon climbed above $70,000.Jackson also dismissed the theory of a four-year bitcoin cycle. Calling it "an old myth that is not confirmed by the data," he said SRX did not incorporate it into the model. He said institutional participation, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and macroeconomic factors now drive prices. He emphasised that "liquidity is more important than anything else."Bitcoin, which peaked around $126,000 last year, stayed in a downtrend for several months. Jackson said that once it exits a downtrend, it does not immediately turn down again.He also cited as a positive factor that Strategy’s perpetual preferred stock STRC, issued by the company holding the most bitcoin, recovered to around its $100 par value. STRC slipped to $72 this summer, but closed at $99.58 on the day. Jackson said Strategy had regained a funding channel and could continue buying bitcoin. He took a sceptical view of other companies that have followed Strategy’s approach.SRX is pursuing a hedged multi-asset digital-asset treasury strategy through its in-house fund SRXH. Jackson said, "Why not build a model that predicts price direction and hedge?" He cited the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and global liquidity as key variables.

extraction.body: Eric Jackson, Head of SRX Global Asset Management, stated that Bitcoin could reach $100,000 by the end of 2026. According to Jackson, if the recent upward breakout in Bitcoin continues, it seems possible that the bullish trend will be maintained for the remainder of the year. Speaking to Coinage, Jackson stated that his company's Bitcoin macro model tracks interest rates, global liquidity, gold-Bitcoin correlation, and other macroeconomic indicators. He explained that the model does not aim to predict short-term daily movements, but rather classifies the market regime over approximately 30 days as a "bullish," "mixed," or "stressed" market. Jackson stated that the model signaled a stressful market on May 26th when Bitcoin was around $77,000, after which the price fell to around $58,000 in the following weeks. However, he noted that the model shifted back to a "mixed" market on August 14th, and then to a "bullish" market a few days later, with Bitcoin quickly rising from around $64,000 to over $70,000. According to the experienced investor, global liquidity is one of the most important variables for Bitcoin. Jackson argued that investors should focus specifically on liquidity conditions and macroeconomic developments rather than getting lost among numerous market indicators. While acknowledging the importance of ETF inflows, Jackson stated that they are not the sole factor determining price direction. Highlighting Bitcoin's strong recovery in August, Jackson noted that in the past, once Bitcoin started moving in a certain direction, it was able to maintain that trend for months. Believing that Bitcoin, after falling from its peak of around $126,000 last year to $58,000, has now initiated a new upward movement, Jackson stated that if the current trend continues, $100,000 could be reached by the end of the year. Jackson said, “As a human being, not a machine, I think Bitcoin is heading towards $100,000 by the end of this year.” However, he cautioned against making such a prediction, stating that he would continue to monitor both his own investor biases and the signals from price charts and models. Jackson also stated that he sees continued ETF inflows in the short term as a positive signal. He specifically noted that capital flows into spot Bitcoin ETFs are one of the key indicators of both individual and institutional investor participation. On the macroeconomic front, Jackson stated that US 10-year Treasury yields and global liquidity indicators should be closely monitored, arguing that declines in bond yields or oil prices could be supportive for Bitcoin and the cryptocurrency market in general. Jackson's long-term outlook for Bitcoin is much higher. He sees Bitcoin as a global collateral asset in the digital economy of the future, and has a highly ambitious price target of $50 million for Bitcoin over the next 15 years. However, he specifically emphasized that this rise will not be linear, and that significant price fluctuations and sharp corrections are possible throughout the process. *This is not investment advice.

extraction.body: Investors will find it challenging to identify a better-performing asset than Bitcoin ( BTC +0.11% ) . Over the past 15 years, the world's first cryptocurrency has skyrocketed more than 1,600,000% (as of Sept. 29). A $10,000 investment made back then would be worth nearly $164 million today. But the volatility is what grabs headlines. At the low point in 2026 on July 1, Bitcoin was trading 53% off its peak. It has bounced back nicely, now trading at roughly $84,171. The bulls are starting to make some noise, wondering whether the bear market is in the past. Can Bitcoin rise 19% to get to $100,000 by the end of the year? Bitcoin doesn't operate in a vacuum. It's a global financial asset. Consequently, it can be influenced by a variety of factors. Macroeconomic headwinds are one of them. The Federal Reserve recently raised its benchmark federal funds rate for the first time in over three years, with more hikes potentially on the table . Chairman Kevin Warsh has expressed that his focus is on controlling inflation, which has been spurred by higher energy prices this year due to the Middle East conflict. This could present a headwind. All else being equal, riskier assets like Bitcoin perform better during an accommodative monetary backdrop. Lower interest rates incentivize greater borrowing by consumers and companies. And they push investors toward financial instruments that might not pay income now, but that promise greater capital appreciation in the future. Artificial intelligence (AI) could be another headwind. While Bitcoin continues to slowly establish itself as a prominent investment asset and potential payment mechanism, it mirrors other cryptocurrencies, as it's most exposed to shifting market sentiment. The AI boom has captivated the investment community, diverting attention away from Bitcoin. And so much capital has gone into AI stocks that might otherwise have flowed into digital assets. Even considering those headwinds, I think it's likely that Bitcoin will reach $100,000 before 2026 ends. That six-figure target is only 19% higher than the current price. That's a small jump for such a high-octane asset. It wouldn't be at all surprising to see crypto maintain its current momentum, as it is known to deliver huge gains. Bitcoin's price follows a four-year cycle, with roughly 48 months between bull-market highs and bear-market lows. The last bear-market low was established in November 2022. If this trend holds, it suggests there's a good chance that Bitcoin's bear market is over and that the march higher has begun. And according to Carson Group's Ryan Detrick, October and November during a midterm election year are the S&P 500 index's two highest-returning months. Since the stock market and Bitcoin have a strong positive correlation, this bodes well for the latter's prospects in the very near term. This is another data point that supports investor optimism. extraction.body: Eric Jackson (에릭 잭슨), chief investment officer at AI-based investment firm SRX Global, forecast bitcoin could reach $100,000 (about 140 million won) by year-end, Coinage reported on Sept. 30 local time.In an interview with the outlet, Jackson said it was "on a trajectory toward $100,000 by year-end" and added, "Ignore the news headlines." He said bitcoin’s bullish breakout had become strong enough to persist despite a recent correction.He pointed to SRX’s bitcoin model. The model combines correlations with assets such as interest rates, global liquidity and gold to divide the market into bullish, mixed and risk phases. It is designed to gauge direction over roughly 30-day periods rather than tomorrow’s price.The model flashed a risk signal on May 26. Bitcoin later fell to $58,000 and then traded sideways through the summer. Bitcoin soon climbed above $70,000.Jackson also dismissed the theory of a four-year bitcoin cycle. Calling it "an old myth that is not confirmed by the data," he said SRX did not incorporate it into the model. He said institutional participation, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and macroeconomic factors now drive prices. He emphasised that "liquidity is more important than anything else."Bitcoin, which peaked around $126,000 last year, stayed in a downtrend for several months. Jackson said that once it exits a downtrend, it does not immediately turn down again.He also cited as a positive factor that Strategy’s perpetual preferred stock STRC, issued by the company holding the most bitcoin, recovered to around its $100 par value. STRC slipped to $72 this summer, but closed at $99.58 on the day. Jackson said Strategy had regained a funding channel and could continue buying bitcoin. He took a sceptical view of other companies that have followed Strategy’s approach.SRX is pursuing a hedged multi-asset digital-asset treasury strategy through its in-house fund SRXH. Jackson said, "Why not build a model that predicts price direction and hedge?" He cited the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield and global liquidity as key variables.

extraction.body: Eric Jackson, Head of SRX Global Asset Management, stated that Bitcoin could reach $100,000 by the end of 2026. According to Jackson, if the recent upward breakout in Bitcoin continues, it seems possible that the bullish trend will be maintained for the remainder of the year. Speaking to Coinage, Jackson stated that his company's Bitcoin macro model tracks interest rates, global liquidity, gold-Bitcoin correlation, and other macroeconomic indicators. He explained that the model does not aim to predict short-term daily movements, but rather classifies the market regime over approximately 30 days as a "bullish," "mixed," or "stressed" market. Jackson stated that the model signaled a stressful market on May 26th when Bitcoin was around $77,000, after which the price fell to around $58,000 in the following weeks. However, he noted that the model shifted back to a "mixed" market on August 14th, and then to a "bullish" market a few days later, with Bitcoin quickly rising from around $64,000 to over $70,000. According to the experienced investor, global liquidity is one of the most important variables for Bitcoin. Jackson argued that investors should focus specifically on liquidity conditions and macroeconomic developments rather than getting lost among numerous market indicators. While acknowledging the importance of ETF inflows, Jackson stated that they are not the sole factor determining price direction. Highlighting Bitcoin's strong recovery in August, Jackson noted that in the past, once Bitcoin started moving in a certain direction, it was able to maintain that trend for months. Believing that Bitcoin, after falling from its peak of around $126,000 last year to $58,000, has now initiated a new upward movement, Jackson stated that if the current trend continues, $100,000 could be reached by the end of the year. Jackson said, “As a human being, not a machine, I think Bitcoin is heading towards $100,000 by the end of this year.” However, he cautioned against making such a prediction, stating that he would continue to monitor both his own investor biases and the signals from price charts and models. Jackson also stated that he sees continued ETF inflows in the short term as a positive signal. He specifically noted that capital flows into spot Bitcoin ETFs are one of the key indicators of both individual and institutional investor participation. On the macroeconomic front, Jackson stated that US 10-year Treasury yields and global liquidity indicators should be closely monitored, arguing that declines in bond yields or oil prices could be supportive for Bitcoin and the cryptocurrency market in general. Jackson's long-term outlook for Bitcoin is much higher. He sees Bitcoin as a global collateral asset in the digital economy of the future, and has a highly ambitious price target of $50 million for Bitcoin over the next 15 years. However, he specifically emphasized that this rise will not be linear, and that significant price fluctuations and sharp corrections are possible throughout the process. *This is not investment advice.

extraction.body: The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’ Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives. “It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest ​people in the world signed that, and ​I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week. “The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests. While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth. The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment. The document outlines four “layers of controls and audits” for AI companies. The first involves implementing internal safety monitoring during training – something that already exists at major labs and has failed to prevent testing failures thus far. The second calls for empowering an internal team to make sure the first layer of monitoring is operating correctly, while the third agrees to give an external auditor the ability to independently assess safety controls. Finally, the agreement calls for companies to designate an independent board to review reports about those safety controls. None of the controls listed in the agreement involve government regulators or include a commitment to publicly detail the findings of independent evaluations. The agreement also appears to allow companies to pick their own evaluators, appoint their own oversight boards and decide whether to publish their results. Trump made the remarks after holding a luncheon with tech leaders including Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO; Mark Zuckerberg , the Meta CEO; Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia; Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO; and other top industry executives. The tech industry, which has largely aligned itself with the Trump administration, has lobbied against strict regulatory oversight, arguing that it would stifle the economy. Zuckerberg, flanked by Trump and other tech moguls, told a press conference after the lunch that he was proud of the agreement and said that it was created to assure the American public that their technology was trustworthy. “This is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. “It was sort of a historic conversation.”

passages: Trump announced that the US government would formally adopt the terminology “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence,” characterising the existing terminology as inadequate and inaccurate for describing contemporary technological capabilities.

US President Donald Trump utilised his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran whilst simultaneously issuing a dramatic ultimatum regarding potential future military action.

Addressing world leaders, Trump stated: “From this point forward, all of the United States documents and hopefully the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial.
Trump declared: “We will only encourage super intelligence.

We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.” This positioning established the Trump administration as fundamentally opposed to regulatory restraints on artificial intelligence development, framing safety mechanisms as impediments to American technological dominance rather than prudent precautionary measures.

Trump predicted that a comprehensive peace agreement with Iran would materialise following the US midterm elections scheduled for 3 November 2026, when the composition of Congress will be fundamentally altered through nationwide voting.

Sunday Guardian Live By: Zaini Majeed Last Updated: September 22, 2026 23:03:26 IST US President Donald Trump utilised his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran whilst simultaneously issuing a dramatic ultimatum regarding potential future military action. Speaking before assembled world leaders, Trump warned he could “annihilate” Iran without achieving a peace agreement, establishing an extraordinarily provocative negotiating posture that positioned military annihilation as a credible policy option contingent upon diplomatic failure. Trump predicted that a comprehensive peace agreement with Iran would materialise following the US midterm elections scheduled for 3 November 2026, when the composition of Congress will be fundamentally altered through nationwide voting. This assertion positioned Trump’s diplomatic timeline directly parallel to domestic electoral cycles, suggesting that post-election congressional configuration would provide enhanced negotiating flexibility or domestic political authority for achieving Iranian concessions previously unobtainable. Trump announced that the US government would formally adopt the terminology “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence,” characterising the existing terminology as inadequate and inaccurate for describing contemporary technological capabilities. Addressing world leaders, Trump stated: “From this point forward, all of the United States documents and hopefully the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial. So it’s super intelligence.” The US president simultaneously dismissed mounting international concerns regarding artificial intelligence safety protocols as a deliberate hoax perpetrated by political adversaries. Trump declared: “We will only encourage super intelligence. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.” This positioning established the Trump administration as fundamentally opposed to regulatory restraints on artificial intelligence development, framing safety mechanisms as impediments to American technological dominance rather than prudent precautionary measures. Regarding Russia’s ongoing military invasion of Ukraine, Trump articulated an optimistic assessment substantially at variance with prevailing international assessments of conflict resolution timelines. Trump stated: “We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done,” adding, “It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand.” This characterisation positioned Trump as an active diplomatic intermediary capable of expediting resolution through direct engagement with both Russian and Ukrainian leadership, implicitly suggesting that previous international diplomatic efforts had proven inadequate and that his personal involvement would produce accelerated outcomes. Trump articulated a comprehensive critique of international institutions and multilateral governance frameworks, declaring that “there is no global government” and that whilst he serves as president, “there will be no global taxes.” The US president announced a trilateral security agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, establishing two military bases whilst prohibiting US adversaries from establishing military presence or making sensitive investments within Greenland’s territory.

extraction.body: The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’ Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives. “It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest ​people in the world signed that, and ​I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week. “The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests. While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth. The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment. The document outlines four “layers of controls and audits” for AI companies. The first involves implementing internal safety monitoring during training – something that already exists at major labs and has failed to prevent testing failures thus far. The second calls for empowering an internal team to make sure the first layer of monitoring is operating correctly, while the third agrees to give an external auditor the ability to independently assess safety controls. Finally, the agreement calls for companies to designate an independent board to review reports about those safety controls. None of the controls listed in the agreement involve government regulators or include a commitment to publicly detail the findings of independent evaluations. The agreement also appears to allow companies to pick their own evaluators, appoint their own oversight boards and decide whether to publish their results. Trump made the remarks after holding a luncheon with tech leaders including Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO; Mark Zuckerberg , the Meta CEO; Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia; Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO; and other top industry executives. The tech industry, which has largely aligned itself with the Trump administration, has lobbied against strict regulatory oversight, arguing that it would stifle the economy. Zuckerberg, flanked by Trump and other tech moguls, told a press conference after the lunch that he was proud of the agreement and said that it was created to assure the American public that their technology was trustworthy. “This is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. “It was sort of a historic conversation.”

Speaking before assembled world leaders, Trump warned he could “annihilate” Iran without achieving a peace agreement, establishing an extraordinarily provocative negotiating posture that positioned military annihilation as a credible policy option contingent upon diplomatic failure. Trump predicted that a comprehensive peace agreement with Iran would materialise following the US midterm elections scheduled for 3 November 2026, when the composition of Congress will be fundamentally altered through nationwide voting. This assertion positioned Trump’s diplomatic timeline directly parallel to domestic electoral cycles, suggesting that post-election congressional configuration would provide enhanced negotiating flexibility or domestic political authority for achieving Iranian concessions previously unobtainable. Trump announced that the US government would formally adopt the terminology “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence,” characterising the existing terminology as inadequate and inaccurate for describing contemporary technological capabilities. Addressing world leaders, Trump stated: “From this point forward, all of the United States documents and hopefully the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial. So it’s super intelligence.” The US president simultaneously dismissed mounting international concerns regarding artificial intelligence safety protocols as a deliberate hoax perpetrated by political adversaries. Trump declared: “We will only encourage super intelligence. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.” This positioning established the Trump administration as fundamentally opposed to regulatory restraints on artificial intelligence development, framing safety mechanisms as impediments to American technological dominance rather than prudent precautionary measures. Regarding Russia’s ongoing military invasion of Ukraine, Trump articulated an optimistic assessment substantially at variance with prevailing international assessments of conflict resolution timelines. Trump stated: “We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done,” adding, “It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand.” This characterisation positioned Trump as an active diplomatic intermediary capable of expediting resolution through direct engagement with both Russian and Ukrainian leadership, implicitly suggesting that previous international diplomatic efforts had proven inadequate and that his personal involvement would produce accelerated outcomes. Trump articulated a comprehensive critique of international institutions and multilateral governance frameworks, declaring that “there is no global government” and that whilst he serves as president, “there will be no global taxes.” The US president announced a trilateral security agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, establishing two military bases whilst prohibiting US adversaries from establishing military presence or making sensitive investments within Greenland’s territory.

Notably, NEAR (CRYPTO:NEAR) surged by 186.6%, and Arbitrum (CRYPTO:ARB) climbed 137.1%. Bitcoin wrapped up the month at $83,995 on September 30. So, what led to renewed interest in crypto in September, and why did so much of that investment flow to smaller coins rather than Bitcoin? According to Santiment, the turnaround can be traced back to the August inflation report, which came in lower than anticipated. This unexpected news briefly pushed down Treasury yields, making cash and bonds offer lower returns. As a result, some investors redirected their funds toward cryptocurrency. The crypto market reacted more dramatically than the stock market because many traders had taken short positions, expecting prices to fall. When prices began to rise instead, those traders had to buy back coins to limit their losses. Additionally, exchanges liquidated borrowed positions once traders' collateral was depleted, leading to more buy orders and turning modest positive news into a powerful rally. However, a rally fueled by short covering can lose momentum once those positions close. After that, price movement relies on genuine buyers, and Santiment data doesn't clarify how much of Bitcoin's September gain came from forced buying. In September 2026, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) experienced a gain of about 7%. While the S&P 500 index barely changed and gold declined by more than 6%, many other major cryptocurrencies outperformed Bitcoin. Notably, NEAR ( CRYPTO:NEAR ) surged by 186.6%, and Arbitrum ( CRYPTO:ARB ) climbed 137.1%.
Bitcoin wrapped up the month at $83,995 on September 30. So, what led to renewed interest in crypto in September, and why did so much of that investment flow to smaller coins rather than Bitcoin?

According to Santiment, the turnaround can be traced back to the August inflation report, which came in lower than anticipated. This unexpected news briefly pushed down Treasury yields, making cash and bonds offer lower returns. As a result, some investors redirected their funds toward cryptocurrency.

The crypto market reacted more dramatically than the stock market because many traders had taken short positions, expecting prices to fall. When prices began to rise instead, those traders had to buy back coins to limit their losses. Additionally, exchanges liquidated borrowed positions once traders’ collateral was depleted, leading to more buy orders and turning modest positive news into a powerful rally.

However, a rally fueled by short covering can lose momentum once those positions close. After that, price movement relies on genuine buyers, and Santiment data doesn’t clarify how much of Bitcoin’s September gain came from forced buying.

Bitcoin’s recent rally saw many buyers eager to own the asset. During a five-day period from September 21 to September 25, US spot Bitcoin ETFs attracted around $2.4 billion , though daily inflows decreased from $999 million to $134 million.

Additionally, Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), known for holding Bitcoin as its primary treasury asset, bought 1,665 BTC for $143 million in late September, bringing its total holdings to 847,666 BTC, valued at about $71.2 billion by month-end. These institutional and corporate buyers provided a more stable base for Bitcoin’s rise compared to the forced buying that characterized smaller coins.

As market fears subsided, investors began reallocating capital into smaller coins, causing Bitcoin’s share of the total crypto market to drop to 58.4% of the $2.88 trillion market cap. Other significant cryptocurrencies also outpaced Bitcoin during this period, with Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) up 9.8%, XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) up 9.9%, and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) up 16.2%, per CoinGecko’s 30-day data, which put Bitcoin’s return at just 7.7%.

While triple-digit gains for smaller coins reflect volatility rather than underlying project strength, coins like NEAR, Arbitrum, and Zcash can swing wildly in both directions. Thus, a significant short-term return does not guarantee long-term potential.
Overall, Bitcoin is still down year-to-date, down 4.5% for 2026 and 26.7% over the past 12 months. September’s performance appears to be a temporary bounce within a larger downward trend.

The surge in smaller coins may be the weakest part of September’s recovery. Their significant gains largely came from a market heavily filled with short positions, and once those short trades close, forced buying should stop. In contrast, Bitcoin has stronger backing from institutional and corporate investors.

However, the relief from tightening interest rates may not last. Following the Fed’s rate hike on September 16 , futures traders currently foresee a 64% probability of another increase at the next meeting on October 27-28 .

If Bitcoin’s market share rises above 58.4% while NEAR and Arbitrum surrender their gains, it might signal an end to this rotation. Conversely, if Bitcoin continues to attract large inflows into spot ETFs while its market share decreases, we’ll have to see if the smaller coins that outperformed Bitcoin in September 2026 can maintain their lead into October.

Microsoft generally available Azure Container Apps Express this week, a deployment model that drops the environment provisioning step and replaces most configuration with opinionated defaults. The launch ships with GA of Azure Container Apps Sandboxes, the isolated compute layer Express runs on. Azure Container Apps and Microsoft's documentation describe the service. Express takes a container image, a region, and application configuration, then provisions compute, ingress, and scaling itself. Apps run on consumption CPU with per-second billing, scale to zero when idle, and pay no environment provisioning fee. Microsoft positions Express as developer-first and agent-first. The second label carries more weight. AI-assisted workflows create and update apps faster than a person configures infrastructure, so the platform removes the configuration surface those workflows touch. The speed comes from underneath. Microsoft's documentation states Express is built entirely on Container Apps Sandboxes, a platform primitive that provisions from prewarmed pools for subsecond startup, isolates each workload in its own hardware-isolated microVM boundary, and bursts to thousands of concurrent sandboxes. Sandboxes support suspend and resume. They snapshot full state including memory and disk, then restore in under a second. Teams can call Sandboxes directly instead of going through Express. Microsoft positions the primitive for agent platforms and secure code-execution services. The top-level ARM resource is Microsoft.App/SandboxGroups , a management boundary for sandboxes that share configuration, comparable to a Container Apps environment. Reddit suggests the primitive shipped long before this announcement. Commenter MuhBlockchain said ACA Sandboxes underpin core Azure services including Foundry Hosted Agents, a detail Microsoft's own material does not state. Commenter tankerkiller125real wrote that his team runs them as Python sandboxes for a customer-facing agent harness. Commenter Minute_Passion_8077 described deploying them for clients through Bicep: point the template at an image, scale to zero when the work stops. Commenter brianveldman drew the line at lifecycle. ACA Jobs run to completion and fit batch processing. Sandboxes provide programmable, isolated compute with lifecycle control. Commenter RustOnTheEdge questioned the hardware-isolated microVM claim without elaborating. Commenter HgnX asked whether Azure Kubernetes Service offers the same capability, noting his team runs AKS for requirements Container Apps does not meet. Microsoft had not answered that question by publication. The pairing matches Google's approach this year. Google Kubernetes Engine combines Pod snapshots, which checkpoint CPU and GPU memory through gVisor, with GKE Agent Sandbox for running untrusted agent code. Microsoft pairs microVM isolation with snapshot-based suspend and resume. Both vendors answer the same design problem: hand an agent an isolated environment that costs nothing while idle and returns in under a second. Express itself is the opinionated application layer on top. It offers a focused subset of Container Apps capabilities: The exclusions define where Express stops. No custom domains, zone redundancy, Key Vault secret references, Easy Auth, OpenTelemetry, Dapr, jobs, workload profiles, GPU workloads, multiple revisions with traffic splitting, or system-assigned managed identities. Service discovery is absent, so apps talk through public URLs. Ingress stays HTTP only. Outbound subnets cannot change once set, and per-replica storage carries constraints. Microsoft advises a standard Container Apps environment when teams need more control over networking, GPU compute, advanced configuration, or environment-level features such as Dapr. The documentation also lists rapid prototyping as an Express fit, where teams build quickly and keep running in production without replatforming. For a workload that needs a custom domain, zone redundancy, or Key Vault-backed secrets, those two statements point different directions. Access is narrower than standard Container Apps. Express requires a Microsoft Entra ID-backed account and rejects personal Microsoft accounts. Teams manage Express through containerapps.azure.com and Sandboxes through sandboxes.azure.com. Commenter MuhBlockchain said those interfaces do not replace the Azure portal. "It's just a separate view, though with a lot more detail. You'll still be able to manage them through the regular portal experience to." Teams with existing standard environments can migrate. Archive the current environment, then restore it as Express. Microsoft says the process preserves app and environment configuration, takes about 15 minutes, and leaves the consumption-free grant intact. The FAQ mentions an opt-out form in the migration notice for organizations that need additional approval or coordination, and warns that inactive environments with no running apps or jobs and no recent activity may get archived and put to sleep. Express reaches more than 40 Azure regions at GA, covering almost every public region where Container Apps runs. Microsoft said customers created thousands of Express apps during public preview and that feedback from those deployments set priorities for this release. For platform teams, the tradeoff sits in the gap between what Express removes and what it still costs. Consumption CPU with per-second billing and scale to zero makes idle agent environments cheap. GPU workloads, service discovery, Dapr, Key Vault integration, and custom domains all require the standard environment. Teams choose the side based on which capabilities the workload needs. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL now reads Apache Iceberg and Parquet files straight from Amazon S3 without ETL pipelines. DuckDB runs inside Aurora, so you can join live transactions with historical lake data through standard PostgreSQL syntax. Microsoft halted infrastructure servicing on its Azure network after maintenance activity Wednesday night disrupted VPN gateways, ExpressRoute connectivity, and VMware-based hybrid clouds across 18 regions. Redmond reported the incident mitigated by Thursday morning and has not identified the root cause. Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. Modern architectures often use legacy services for specific tasks, but these services may lack accurate documentation and using them can be risky if you don't understand them well. passages: Read original story MetaMask Lido Validators Exit After Infrastructure Compromise by Ahmed Barakat at Cryptonews.com

MetaMask Staking, formerly known as ConsenSys Staking, is on Lido as the operator began exiting its Ethereum validators from the protocol after investigating an infrastructure compromise, according to a Lido governance forum disclosure.
The complete exit, withdrawal, and re-entry cycle could take up to approximately 45 days, while MetaMask says it has found no immediate threat to its wallets.
In 2023, the same operator, then operating under the Consensys name, mistakenly exited 125 Lido validators and compensated stakers for lost rewards.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

In September 2025, staking provider Kiln exited 5,726 validators across networks after a compromised GitHub token enabled an attacker to access its infrastructure; Lido later estimated that the exits cost about 207 ETH in missed protocol rewards.
In a user update posted a few hours ago, MetaMask said it was responding to an ongoing security incident affecting part of its infrastructure.
Lido expects the final affected validators to be exited, but not fully withdrawn, by the end of October 7.
The exit can still carry a cost: affected validators may forgo rewards, and taking them offline before they complete the exit could bring downtime penalties if done to reduce network-penalty risks.
MetaMask and Lido say a full investigation is underway and that they will share further updates as available.
The key unresolved questions are which part of MetaMask's infrastructure was compromised and whether the issue extended beyond the staking operation.
The incident adds to the operational risks facing crypto infrastructure, where a security problem at a service provider can trigger disruption even without a disclosed protocol exploit.
The number of affected validators and the quantity of ETH involved have not been made public as of now.
MetaMask signs for the validators it operates, but says it does not manage clients' withdrawal keys, so the operator cannot move the underlying stake on their behalf.
Ethereum's validator queues also shape how quickly stake can return to active service, a consideration for the wider Ethereum ecosystem .
